---
title: "Same Data, Different Estimators"
date: "2026-05-13"
---

## One panel, several questions

The BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS) county file is a useful
benchmark panel because it is large, public, and substantively familiar. It has
monthly county unemployment rates, many pre-treatment periods, and a natural
COVID-era policy application: stay-at-home orders in April 2020.

This makes it a good "same data, different estimators" example. Instead of
changing the empirical setting every time we introduce a new panel method, we
can hold the panel fixed and ask what each estimator is doing differently.

The setup follows the application in Shen, Song, and Abadie:

| quantity | value |
| --- | ---: |
| outcome | county unemployment rate |
| data source | BLS LAUS county flat file |
| pre-period | January 2008 to March 2020 |
| post-period | April 2020 |
| control states | Arkansas, Iowa, Nebraska, North Dakota, South Dakota, Utah, Wyoming |
| treated units | counties in stay-at-home-order states |
| excluded units | Alaska and District of Columbia |
| control counties | 438 |
| treated counties | 2,674 |
| pre-treatment months | 147 |

The paper reports an ATT of about 5.06 percentage points. With the current BLS
flat file and the code below, `MSC.jl` constructs the same-sized panel and gives
an application-replication estimate of 4.9552 under the default bounded solver
settings.

## Construct the panel once

The key is to build one common panel, then pass exactly the same matrix to
several estimators. The county panel has controls first, treated units second,
pre-treatment periods first, and April 2020 as the only post-treatment period.

The `MSC.jl` example script contains the data-preparation helper, so we can
reuse it rather than duplicating parsing logic:

```julia
using MSC
using SynthDiD
using Statistics

include("/home/xao/projects/software/MSC.jl/examples/03_covid_sah_orders.jl")

df = load_laus_county_panel(find_laus_county_file())
panel = MSC.panel_matrices(df, :county, :month, :unemployment_rate, :D)

Y = Matrix{Float64}(panel.Y)
N0 = panel.N0
T0 = panel.T0
```

Here `N0 = 438`, `size(Y, 1) - N0 = 2674`, and `T0 = 147`.

## Four estimators on the same outcome matrix

Now the same `Y`, `N0`, and `T0` can be passed to several estimators.

```julia
# Plain DiD
tau_did = SynthDiD.did_estimate(Y, N0, T0)

# Synthetic difference-in-differences
tau_sdid = SynthDiD.synthdid_estimate(Y, N0, T0)

# Synthetic control
tau_sc = SynthDiD.sc_estimate(Y, N0, T0)

# Multivariate synthetic control
tau_msc = MSC.msc_estimate(
    panel;
    lambdas = [0.03],
    standardize = false,
    max_iter = 100,
    tol = 1e-4,
)
```

On the downloaded BLS file, this gives:

| estimator | estimate |
| --- | ---: |
| Difference-in-differences | 2.6940 |
| Synthetic difference-in-differences | 2.6944 |
| Synthetic control | 3.4134 |
| Multivariate synthetic control | 4.9552 |
| Paper benchmark | about 5.06 |

These are not just different implementations of the same estimand. They encode
different ways to decide which controls and which pre-periods matter.

## What changes across estimators?

Plain DiD uses equal unit weights and equal time weights. It asks whether
treated counties changed more from the pre-period average to April 2020 than
the no-order counties did. This is transparent, but it leans heavily on a
parallel-trends comparison between a very large treated group and seven
no-order states.

Synthetic control changes the unit weights. It tries to form a weighted control
group that better matches the treated group before April 2020. In this example
the estimate moves from about 2.69 to about 3.41 percentage points.

Synthetic DiD changes both unit and time weights. In this particular one-month
post-treatment application, the SDiD estimate is almost the same as DiD. That
is itself informative: for this design and implementation, the optimized
weights do not move the simple average comparison much.

Multivariate synthetic control changes the target problem more substantially.
It does not fit one synthetic control for an aggregate treated average, and it
does not fit 2,674 separate synthetic controls. Instead it learns a sparse
matrix mapping 438 control counties to all 2,674 treated counties jointly, then
averages the treated-county effects. That is why it is a natural estimator for
this paper's high-dimensional disaggregated setting.

## Why this example is useful

This panel is a good teaching and diagnostic example because the estimates are
not identical:

| comparison | lesson |
| --- | --- |
| DiD vs SC | unit weights matter |
| DiD vs SDiD | time weights may or may not matter in a one-post-period design |
| SC vs MSC | aggregate treated fit differs from high-dimensional treated-unit fit |
| MSC vs paper | matching sample counts is not the same as pinning the exact data vintage and optimizer |

For applied work, this is the right workflow. Start with a single panel and
force the estimators to use the same sample. Then disagreements are easier to
interpret: they come from the estimator, not from hidden data-processing
differences.

## Practical notes

The BLS data are large enough that I would not make the book render download or
parse the file every time. The better pattern is:

1. keep the raw BLS flat file outside the book repository;
2. write one data-preparation script that produces a common panel object;
3. cache a small summary table of estimates;
4. make the chapter explain the design, code path, and interpretation.

The current `MSC.jl` example does exactly this for the paper application. It
looks for `data/la.data.64.County` or an explicit `BLS_LAUS_COUNTY_FILE`, builds
the paper-sized panel, and prints the comparison with the reported paper
number.

If the goal is exact reproduction of 5.06, the missing ingredient is not
another estimator. It is the paper's exact replication archive: the BLS vintage,
county inclusion file, and optimizer/tuning settings. Without that archive, the
honest claim is that we replicate the application design and sample counts, and
we report how different estimators behave on the same public data.
